## Dense helpers and the pivoted Gaussian solve (`dsolve_lu`) {#sec-ch10-dense}

### Summary

The per-cell solvers of kintera work on small dense matrices stored as plain row-major arrays. A set of helpers does
the vector and matrix products they need. One function, `dsolve_lu`, solves a square system by Gaussian elimination
with partial pivoting. It is the first solve of the implicit kinetics step and of the constrained Newton step, and
it reports an exactly singular matrix so that the caller can fall back to a least-squares solve.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Solve $\mathsf A x = b$ in place for a small dense $\mathsf A$, @eq-ch10-dense-elimination.

**Data.** Row-major $n \times n$ array and length-$n$ vector, destroyed and overwritten.

**Placement.** Inside per-cell kernels, on CPU or CUDA (@sec-ch12).

**Activation.** Always; no option.

**Guarantee / limits.** Fails only on an exactly zero pivot; no condition estimate.

**Evidence.** Indirect, through `test_thermo`; see the Tests layer.
:::

Local symbols: $\mathsf A$, an $n \times n$ matrix with entries $a_{ik}$; $b$, the right-hand side; $x$, the
solution; $k$, the elimination step; $f_{ik}$, the multiplier of row $i$ at step $k$.

### Derivation

At step $k$ the row with the largest $|a_{ik}|$, $i \ge k$, is swapped into row $k$ together with $b_k$. Then each
lower row is reduced:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{ik} &= a_{ik} / a_{kk} \\
a_{ij} &\leftarrow a_{ij} - f_{ik}\, a_{kj} \\
b_i &\leftarrow b_i - f_{ik}\, b_k
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch10-dense-elimination}

for $i > k$ and $j > k$. Back substitution then gives, for $i = n-1$ down to $0$,

$$
x_i = \frac{1}{a_{ii}} \Big( b_i - \sum_{j > i} a_{ij}\, x_j \Big) .
$$ {#eq-ch10-dense-back}

@eq-ch10-dense-elimination and @eq-ch10-dense-back are computed in `dsolve_lu`
({{< code src/math/core.h dsolve_lu >}}). Four steps explain what the method guarantees.

*Step 1: elimination is a factorization.* Step $k$ subtracts $f_{ik}$ times row $k$ from each row $i > k$. That is
a left multiplication by the unit lower-triangular matrix $\mathsf L_k = \mathsf I - f_k e_k^{\mathrm T}$, with
$f_k = (0, \dots, 0, f_{k+1,k}, \dots, f_{n-1,k})^{\mathrm T}$. The row swap is a permutation $\mathsf P_k$. After
$n$ steps the matrix is upper triangular, $\mathsf U = \mathsf L_{n-1}\mathsf P_{n-1} \cdots \mathsf L_0 \mathsf P_0
\mathsf A$, which rearranges to

$$
\mathsf P \mathsf A = \mathsf L \mathsf U ,
$$ {#eq-ch10-dense-plu}

with $\mathsf P$ the product of the swaps and $\mathsf L$ unit lower triangular with entries $f_{ik}$. The same
operations applied to $b$ give $\mathsf L^{-1}\mathsf P b$, and @eq-ch10-dense-back solves $\mathsf U x =
\mathsf L^{-1}\mathsf P b$.

*Step 2: why partial pivoting.* The pivot is the largest $|a_{ik}|$ in its column, so every multiplier obeys
$|f_{ik}| \le 1$. Each update in @eq-ch10-dense-elimination then grows an entry by at most the size of the pivot row,
and the computed $x$ solves a nearby system $(\mathsf A + \delta\mathsf A)x = b$ with $\lVert\delta\mathsf A\rVert$
a small multiple of $\epsilon\lVert\mathsf A\rVert$ times the growth factor, which is modest in practice (Higham
2002, chapter 9).[^ch10-dense-refs] Without pivoting a small pivot gives multipliers of any size and no such bound.

*Step 3: what the singularity test detects.* `dsolve_lu` returns `false` only when the largest remaining entry of a
column is exactly zero. Scaling $\mathsf A$ by any nonzero factor scales every candidate pivot by the same factor, so
the test does not depend on units. It is not a rank test. A matrix that is singular in exact arithmetic usually
produces a round-off pivot, not an exact zero, and is then solved with a huge $x$. Whether the pivot of a given
singular matrix comes out exactly zero depends on the rounding of the platform.

*Step 4: when the fallback runs.* The implicit kinetics step calls `psolve` only when `dsolve_lu` returns `false`
({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_impl.h >}}), that is only on an exactly zero pivot, the same rule as LAPACK
`getrf`. `check_ch10_dense.py` measures all four statements:[^ch10-dense-check]

- "(a) dsolve_lu, 300 random systems n=2..8: max normwise backward error 1.31e-16 (tol 64 eps = 1.4e-14); max forward
  error / cond 2.13e-16 vs numpy.linalg.solve (tol 1e-13) PASS"
- "(b1) dsolve_lu returns false on an exactly singular 2x2 (True) and true on a regular matrix scaled by 1e-300 (x err
  2.8e-17) PASS"
- "(b2) rank-1 3x3 (numerically singular, round-off pivots): dsolve_lu returns True, max|x| = 3.5e+17; no fallback to
  psolve is triggered for this case INFO". That is the committed run. On a clean x86_64 build of the pin (GCC 11.5.0)
  the same matrix gives an exact zero pivot: "dsolve_lu returns False, max|x| = 2.7e+00"
  (`src/kintera_report/ch10/runs/check_ch10_dense_x86_64.out`, which records the build; the rest of the line is fixed
  text of the script). The outcome is decided by rounding, as step 3 says.

### Numerical method

The elimination runs column by column with no scaling of rows. A column whose largest remaining magnitude is exactly
zero ends the solve with `false`; any nonzero pivot, however small, is accepted. The multipliers are not stored, so
the factorization cannot be reused for another right-hand side. The figure is not provided: the figure module is not
written yet.

### Code

| what | code link | symbol | switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| pivoted solve | {{< code src/math/core.h dsolve_lu >}} | `dsolve_lu` | always |
| products | {{< code src/math/core.h mmdot >}} | `mmdot` | always |
| matrix-vector product | {{< code src/math/core.h mvdot >}} | `mvdot` | always |
| $\mathsf A^{\mathrm T} \mathsf A$ | {{< code src/math/core.h matmul_ATA >}} | `matmul_ATA` | always |
| swaps | {{< code src/math/swap.h swap_cols_safe >}} | `swap_cols_safe` | always |

: Code map of the dense helpers. {#tbl-ch10-dense-code}

1. `core.h` also holds `set_identity`, `vvdot`, `norm2`, `normalize`, `mvdot_t`; `swap.h` holds
   `swap_cols`, `swap_cols_safe`, `swap_vals` and `swap_rows`. All are templates marked for host and device.
2. The implicit kinetics step of @sec-ch06 builds $\mathsf I/\Delta t - \mathsf S \mathsf J$ with `mmdot` and calls
   `dsolve_lu`; if it returns `false`, the step falls back to `psolve` of @sec-ch10-pseudo-inverse
   ({{< code src/kinetics/evolve_implicit_impl.h >}}).
3. `constrained_newton_step` of @sec-ch10-newton calls `dsolve_lu` first.

### Limits

- `mmdot_t` is not an API at this pin ({{< code src/math/core.h >}}).[^ch10-dense-k20] Its removal does not
  establish numerical correctness of a transpose-product implementation; check (f) records absence.
- `swap_cols` carries the comment "no-op trick won't work; do normal swap" next to a comma expression. Read under
  C++17 sequencing rules, the expression does swap the two columns; this is a hypothesis, not tested. It has no
  caller; `psolve` uses `swap_cols_safe` ({{< code src/math/swap.h swap_cols >}}).
- `swap_rows` takes a row count `m` that it does not use.
- `set_identity`, `vvdot`, `norm2`, `normalize`, `mvdot_t`, `swap_cols`, `swap_rows` and `swap_vals` have no caller
  outside `src/math` at the pin (searched by name; `normalize` also matches unrelated words).
- `dsolve_lu` gives no warning for a nearly singular matrix: its test detects only an exactly zero pivot (step 3).
- `core.h` calls `fabs` and `sqrt` without including `<cmath>`; it compiles only where a header included before it
  provides them (spec suspect S10-6; the check harness includes `<cmath>` first).
